questions.stem: Which airline operates the world's largest dedicated freighter fleet by number of aircraft?
options: FedEx Express
Emirates SkyCargo
UPS Airlines
Korean Air Cargo
questions.why: FedEx Express has operated the world's largest dedicated cargo airline fleet for decades, with over 700 aircraft.
questions.deepDive: FedEx Express pioneered the hub-and-spoke air express model with its Memphis SuperHub, operating Boeing 777Fs, 767Fs, and MD-11Fs. Its dominance comes from vertical integration — it owns both the aircraft and the ground delivery network, capturing economics across the full chain. Emirates SkyCargo is the world's largest international cargo airline by belly-hold plus freighter volume, creating a common misconception. UPS is the second-largest dedicated freighter fleet. Air cargo represents roughly 35% of global trade value while moving only 1-2% by volume — it's the high-value, time-sensitive tier of global logistics. Dedicated freighters are distinct from belly cargo carried on passenger aircraft, which provides most of the world's long-haul air freight capacity.

questions.stem: At an airport cargo terminal, a 'Unit Load Device' (ULD) is best described as which of the following?
options: The maximum cargo weight per flight permitted by the FAA
A standardized container or pallet designed to interlock with aircraft holds
A software system tracking cargo from warehouse to aircraft
The forklift vehicle used to load cargo into the belly hold
questions.why: ULDs are standardized containers and pallets that make air cargo unitization efficient and enable mechanized aircraft loading.
questions.deepDive: Unit Load Devices come in two main types: containers (igloos, cans) and flat pallets. The most common are LD3s used in widebody belly holds, LD7 pallets, and the large 96x125-inch pallets for main-deck freighters. IATA standardizes ULD dimensions so they interlock with aircraft floor systems, enabling mechanized loading that cut ground times from hours to minutes. Each ULD has a tare weight (60-160kg) counting against payload. IATA manages a global ULD interchange pool. Mis-tagged or damaged ULDs are a leading cause of cargo delays. The shift from break-bulk air freight to unitized ULD loading in the 1960s-70s was as transformative for air cargo as containerization was for ocean shipping.

questions.stem: Ocean Network Express (ONE) was formed in 2018 by merging the container shipping operations of which three Japanese carriers?
options: NYK Line + Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) + K Line
NYK Line + Evergreen + K Line
Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) + K Line + Yang Ming
NYK Line + MOL + COSCO Shipping
questions.why: ONE was formed specifically by NYK, MOL, and K Line consolidating their container units to achieve scale and cut losses.
questions.deepDive: The merger was catalyzed by the 2016 Hanjin Shipping bankruptcy, which shocked the industry and showed that even large carriers could fail spectacularly. Japanese carriers had been losing money for years due to overcapacity and thin margins. By combining, they created a carrier with roughly 7% global market share, ranking 6th worldwide. The integration was rocky — ONE reported a $600M loss in its first year due to IT system migration failures, a cautionary tale in carrier M&A. Today ONE is a profitable mid-tier carrier. The episode illustrates both the logic of consolidation in cyclical industries and the operational hazards: combining three IT systems, cultures, and customer relationships simultaneously is extraordinarily difficult even with strong strategic rationale.

questions.stem: In ocean freight contracting, 'dead freight' is the charge applied when:
options: Cargo exceeds the vessel's declared structural weight limit
A shipper fails to tender the volume of cargo they committed to in a booking
Empty containers must be repositioned from surplus to deficit ports
A vessel arrives late and misses its assigned berth window
questions.why: Dead freight is a revenue-protection charge when a shipper books space but doesn't ship the committed volume.
questions.deepDive: Vessel slots are a perishable asset — if you book 100 TEUs and ship 60, the carrier has 40 empty slots that cannot be recovered. Dead freight compensates for this lost revenue. The charge is typically calculated as the freight that would have been earned on the unshipped cargo minus the variable costs the carrier saved by not carrying it. In practice, dead freight is often negotiated away or reduced under long-term service contracts, and more rigorously enforced in tight markets. It is distinct from demurrage (detention of a vessel beyond agreed laytime), detention (container held beyond free days on land), and port congestion surcharges. Understanding dead freight matters when structuring MQCs (Minimum Quantity Commitments) in annual carrier contracts.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the tradeoff between 'efficient' and 'resilient' supply chain design, and what accelerated the shift in corporate priorities?
options: Efficient chains minimize cost via lean, concentrated sourcing; resilient chains build redundancy — pandemic disruptions and tariff shocks shifted boards from cost to continuity
Resilient chains use AI-driven routing; efficient chains use manual planning — digital transformation drove the shift
Efficient chains maximize warehouse footprint; resilient chains minimize physical inventory — e-commerce drove the shift
Resilient chains near-shore all production; efficient chains fully offshore to lowest-cost labour — rising Asian wages drove the shift
questions.why: The efficiency-resilience tradeoff is the defining strategic tension in post-COVID supply chain design, catalyzed by pandemic and trade shocks.
questions.deepDive: Pre-2020, lean manufacturing and Just-In-Time principles optimized supply chains almost purely for cost. The Toyota Production System stripped every buffer. COVID-19 exposed this fragility — a single Suez blockage, a Wuhan lockdown, or a Taiwan Strait tension could halt global assembly lines. Companies responded by diversifying suppliers via China+1 strategies, increasing safety stock, building regional inventories, and near-shoring. McKinsey estimates resilient chains cost 12-16% more than lean equivalents. The strategic question is how much resilience to buy: companies that over-built resilience now carry expensive excess inventory, as seen in the 2022-23 inventory glut. The right answer is context-dependent: semiconductor supply chains need far more resilience than fast-fashion, because substitution is impossible and lead times are measured in years, not weeks.

questions.stem: Laylat al-Qadr ('Night of Power') holds what significance in Islamic theology?
options: It commemorates the Prophet Muhammad's night ascent through the heavens (Isra and Mi'raj)
It marks the night the first verses of the Quran were revealed to Muhammad
It celebrates Muhammad's migration (Hijra) from Mecca to Medina
It marks the signing of the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah ending the Mecca standoff
questions.why: Laylat al-Qadr is the night of the Quran's first revelation to Muhammad, occurring in the last ten days of Ramadan.
questions.deepDive: Laylat al-Qadr falls in the last ten nights of Ramadan, most commonly believed to be the 27th night, though scholars debate the exact date. The Quran (97:1-5) declares: 'We revealed it on the Night of Power; and what will explain what the Night of Power is? It is better than a thousand months.' This marks Allah's first communication to Muhammad through the angel Jibril (Gabriel), revealing the opening verses of Surah al-Alaq ('Read in the name of your Lord who created...'). Muslims worldwide intensify prayer, Quran recitation, and supplication, believing deeds on this night carry exceptional spiritual weight. Isra and Mi'raj — the night journey and heavenly ascent — is a completely separate event commemorated on the 27th of Rajab, commonly confused with Laylat al-Qadr.

questions.stem: The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis (linguistic relativity) proposes that:
options: Children are born with a Universal Grammar hardwired into human cognition
The structure of a language shapes how its speakers perceive and think about reality
All human languages descended from a single African proto-language
Language acquisition is purely learned behavior with no innate component
questions.why: Sapir-Whorf holds that linguistic structure influences or determines the cognitive categories through which speakers experience the world.
questions.deepDive: The hypothesis exists in strong and weak forms. The strong version (linguistic determinism, associated with Whorf's work on Hopi concepts of time) claims language determines thought — now largely rejected. The weak version (linguistic relativity, Sapir) argues language influences but doesn't determine cognition — supported by modern research. Key experiments: Russian speakers distinguish light-blue (goluboy) from dark-blue (siniy) with separate words and perceive color boundaries faster than English speakers. The Pirahã people of the Amazon lack number words beyond 'few' and 'many,' correlating with difficulty in exact quantity tasks. The debate contrasts sharply with Chomsky's Universal Grammar, which holds that grammatical structures are innate and species-wide. Whorf was an amateur linguist and fire insurance inspector; his Hopi analysis has since been contested.

questions.stem: The Duckworth-Lewis-Stern (DLS) method is used in cricket to do which of the following?
options: Calculate player ratings for ICC Test championship standings
Adjust the target score for the chasing team when rain interrupts a limited-overs match
Determine bowling over allocations and line-up order in T20 matches
Set batting priority for Super Overs in tied T20 internationals
questions.why: DLS is the mathematical method for recalculating fair targets in rain-interrupted ODI and T20 games.
questions.deepDive: Duckworth-Lewis was developed by statisticians Frank Duckworth and Tony Lewis, later updated by Steve Stern (hence DLS). It's built on the concept that each team has two resources: wickets remaining and overs remaining. Rain doesn't simply reduce overs — it removes specific phases of play (powerplay, death overs), affecting run-scoring potential non-linearly. Earlier average run rate methods failed badly when overs were lost mid-innings. DLS replaced them at ICC events from 1999 onwards. It remains controversial — fans often feel revised targets are unfair — but statistically it is vastly superior to simpler methods. The method requires complex resource tables that match officials apply in real time using official software. A common misconception is that DLS always favors the team batting second; it actually recalculates neutrally based on remaining resources.

questions.stem: Netflix releasing all 13 episodes of 'House of Cards' Season 1 simultaneously in February 2013 was culturally significant primarily because:
options: It was the first streaming-original show to win a Primetime Emmy Award
It pioneered the full-season simultaneous drop, igniting the binge-watching era of TV consumption
It introduced 4K Ultra HD streaming to a mass consumer audience for the first time
It was the first television production to use AI-generated screenplay software in development
questions.why: House of Cards was the first major show dropped as a full simultaneous season, triggering the binge-watching cultural shift.
questions.deepDive: Before Netflix's House of Cards on February 1, 2013, all TV — including early streaming — followed the weekly episode model inherited from broadcast schedules. Netflix releasing all 13 episodes at once was a deliberate bet informed by data: subscribers who watched pilot episodes were dramatically more likely to continue if more episodes were immediately available. The word 'binge-watching' spiked in search trends within days. Netflix CEO Reed Hastings later described it as 'giving people what they want.' The model disrupted appointment television, eroded live broadcast viewership, and changed how writers' rooms think about pacing — shows now build episode-to-episode cliffhangers rather than weekly ones. House of Cards winning Emmy nominations that year gave streaming prestige credibility it had previously lacked.

questions.stem: Rousseau's 'General Will' (volonté générale) is best described as:
options: The aggregate sum of all individual citizens' private desires and self-interests
The collective interest of the community as a whole, which may differ from any individual will or even the majority vote
The democratic mandate conferred on a government through popular majority vote
The inherent sovereign authority of a monarch to override parliamentary legislation
questions.why: Rousseau distinguished the general will (the common good) from the will of all (the sum of private interests), which may diverge significantly.
questions.deepDive: Rousseau articulated this in 'The Social Contract' (1762). He argued humans enter a social contract, surrendering individual liberty to the community and receiving civil liberty guided by the general will in return. The general will always aims at the common good — it cannot be wrong by definition, though citizens can be mistaken about what it requires. This creates a notorious paradox: individuals who resist the general will can be 'forced to be free,' a phrase critics from Isaiah Berlin to Jacob Talmon cite as a philosophical precursor to totalitarianism. Rousseau heavily influenced the French Revolution — Robespierre cited him extensively to justify the Terror. Modern democratic theory distinguishes the general will from simple majoritarianism, a distinction crucial for understanding minority rights, constitutional entrenchment, and why democracies protect certain rights even from majority votes.
